title: Prime Fibonacci Numbers Have Prime (or 4) Indices
content: **Module framing.** A *Fibonacci prime* is a prime Fibonacci number ($2, 3, 5, 13, 89, \dots$ at indices $3, 4, 5, 7, 11, \dots$). A basic structural constraint, immediate from the parent entry's index-divisibility law $F_m \mid F_n \iff m \mid n$, is that the index of a Fibonacci prime is itself prime — with the single exception $F_4 = 3$. This entry proves $F_n \text{ prime} \Rightarrow n \text{ prime} \lor n = 4$, pins $n = 4$ as the unique composite escape, and shows the converse fails ($F_{19} = 4181 = 37\cdot 113$ with $19$ prime). It is the standard first observation reducing the (open) search for Fibonacci primes to prime indices.
mathContext: $F_n$ prime $\Rightarrow n$ prime $\lor\ n = 4$; the converse is false.

title: Namespace and the open Nat Number-Theory Layer
content: The `namespace FibonacciIdentitiesOQ02OQ02PrimeIndex` wrapper isolates this child file's lemmas from the parent `FibonacciIdentitiesOQ02.lean`, whose index-divisibility law $F_m \mid F_n \iff m \mid n$ this entry consumes. `open Nat` is what lets the proof name `Nat.Prime`, `Nat.fib`, and the divisor-existence lemmas (`exists_dvd_of_not_prime2`) unqualified — the entire argument lives in $\mathbb{N}$, reasoning about prime versus composite *indices*, so pulling the `Nat` namespace into scope keeps the primality and divisibility statements readable.
mathContext: Scope for $\mathbb{N}$-level reasoning: `Nat.Prime`, `Nat.fib`, and `Nat.exists_dvd_of_not_prime2` become available unqualified.

title: Isolating a Nontrivial Index Divisor (and why 4 is special)
content: `exists_divisor_ge_three` proves every composite $n \neq 4$ has a divisor $d$ with $3 \le d < n$. From `Nat.exists_dvd_of_not_prime2` we get a proper divisor $m$ with $2 \le m < n$; if $m \ge 3$ we use it, and if $m = 2$ (so $n$ is even) the cofactor $n/2$ works — it is $\ge 3$ *exactly because* $n \ne 4$ (an `omega` fact from $n = 2k$). This is the crux: $4$'s only proper divisor above $1$ is $2$, and $F_2 = 1$ is a unit, so no divisor of $4$ lands in the productive $3 \le d < n$ range. Every other composite index has one.

title: The Prime-Index Theorem
content: `fib_prime_imp_index_prime_or_four`: if $F_n$ is prime then $n$ is prime or $n = 4$. Assume otherwise: $n$ composite, $n \ne 4$. Then $F_n$ prime forces $F_n \ge 2$, so $n \ge 3$ (as $F_0, F_1, F_2 \in \{0,1\}$). Take $d$ with $3 \le d < n$, $d \mid n$. The transfer law `Nat.fib_dvd` gives $F_d \mid F_n$; monotonicity `Nat.fib_mono` gives $2 = F_3 \le F_d$; strict monotonicity `Nat.fib_lt_fib` gives $F_d < F_n$ from $d < n$. So $F_n$ has a divisor strictly between $1$ and itself, contradicting primality (`Nat.Prime.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd`).
mathContext: $F_n$ prime, $n$ composite $\neq 4 \Rightarrow 1 < F_d < F_n$ and $F_d \mid F_n$ — contradiction.

title: Corollaries: n ≥ 5 and the Composite-Index Contrapositive
content: Two one-line specializations. `fib_prime_index_prime_of_ge_five`: for $n \ge 5$, $F_n$ prime $\Rightarrow n$ prime outright — the $n = 4$ exception only matters below $5$. `fib_not_prime_of_composite`: a composite index other than $4$ yields a composite Fibonacci number, the contrapositive reading of the main theorem. Together they package the constraint in the two forms most useful for downstream reasoning about Fibonacci primes.
mathContext: $n \ge 5,\ F_n$ prime $\Rightarrow n$ prime; composite $n \neq 4 \Rightarrow F_n$ composite.

title: Sharpness and One-Directionality
content: Two `decide`-checked facts fix the exact scope. **Sharpness:** $F_4 = 3$ is prime while $4$ is composite, so the conclusion genuinely must read '$n$ prime $\lor\ n = 4$' and not just '$n$ prime'; $4$ is the unique such escape. **One-directionality:** $19$ is prime yet $F_{19} = 4181 = 37 \cdot 113$ is composite, so a prime index does *not* force a prime value — the implication has no converse. Both use `decide` (kernel evaluation of `Nat.fib` and `Nat.Prime`), not `native_decide`, so no `Lean.ofReduceBool` is introduced and the entry stays 0-axiom.
